title: Rule-out mechanics: How follow-up observations resolve collision risk
text: It never learned an orbit. What happens next is much older arithmetic. Fit a trajectory then sample every orbit the data still allows. That cloud is the answer. In December, a survey telescope in Chile caught a 60 m rock. Its odds of hitting Earth climbed past 3%, the highest ever recorded. 5 days later, they were essentially zero. Here is why. The uncertainty is a long, thin cloud with Earth inside it. More observations shrink the cloud. So, while Earth is still inside, the odds climb. They collapse once the cloud shrinks past us. Then, the same thing happened to the moon. Its odds climbed for months to the highest value yet. Web finally ruled it out in
